## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.54846.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.54846.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

The manuscript presents a detailed and in-depth study of word processing, providing evidence that a compositional letter code potentially makes a major contribution to word reading and can account for reading of jumbled words. One of the major strengths of this work is the combination of careful behavioral experiments, a simple neural model based on properties of neurons in monkey IT cortex, and fMRI data in human participants.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "A compositional letter code in high-level visual cortex explains how we read jumbled words" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, including Chris I Baker as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Floris de Lange as the Senior Editor.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

The reviewers find the manuscript describes a very interesting and detailed study of the potential contribution of a compositional letter code to word reading using novel approaches across behavioral and neuroimaging data. A simple model of responses to individual letter shapes can explain performance in visual search tasks and capture some aspects of word and non-word processing. Further, neuroimaging data suggests that the compositional letter code corresponds to processing in a region in lateral occipital cortex, with the visual word form area (VWFA) corresponding to processing of properties related to word knowledge. One of the major strengths of this work is the combination of careful behavioral experiments, a simple neural model based on properties of neurons in monkey inferotemporal cortex, and fMRI data in human participants.

While the manuscript is well-written and comprehensive, the reviewers felt there are a number of revisions that would strengthen the work. These revisions would require significant reframing of the manuscript to more accurately reflect the data and the existing literature.

Essential revisions:

1) The conclusions tend to be overstated. The manuscript provides an interesting demonstration of what a visually based model can accomplish, but the authors go too far in their interpretation. The compositional letter code explains aspects of word and non-word processing, but not everything related to word reading. For example, in the lexical decision task, response times for words are explained by word frequency and there will be contributions from semantics, especially when reading strings of words/sentences. The authors should be clearer in describing what the data show and not over-reach into an account of word reading that discounts other factors without justification. This will also require a change in the title of the paper since most of the tasks the authors employ are not about word reading.

2) Related to point (1), the authors make a series of assertions that are not supported by their data and also present an oversimplified and somewhat biased review of the literature. The authors should clarify and justify these assertions. In particular:

a) "we hypothesized that word reading is enabled by a purely visual representation". There is a large and robust literature demonstrating how various linguistic properties have substantial effects on word recognition and the authors should acknowledge and cite this literature.

b) Visual search is very different than reading. It should be made clear that this task is not a test of the more general computations involved in reading.

c) "This difference in visual similarity explains why transposing the middle letters renders a word easier to read than transposing its edge letters". The authors should more clearly explain or qualify this assertion.

d) The two sentences in the Introduction seem to contradict each other. It is first suggested that word reading could be explained by a purely visual code, but then it is stated that reading could be a confound. It seems that what the authors want to say is that many different tasks involving words can (but are not necessarily always) be achieved by visual computations. This is a different claim than what is written throughout the paper.

e) The work as presented is not a test of the hypothesis that cortical regions involved in word recognition have tuning for letter combinations. Evidence for this hypothesis is based on a very different paradigm and the effect has been replicated by at least 3 different labs. The authors should clearly explain how the phenomenon they report aligns with those data.

f) Conceptually it is unclear how the bigram model lines up with the main assertion of the manuscript that performance can be understood in terms of the summation of performance for single letters. As soon as additional weights are added for bigrams isn't this akin to saying that there is a different representation of bigrams than of individual letters?

g) "According to an influential account of word reading…. ". This influential account of word reading is about the word recognition process not the detection of bigrams in a search array. It makes no comment or prediction about how the proposed neurons would be involved in the tasks developed by the authors. This is not to say that the model of bigram detectors in word-selective cortex is correct, just that the present work can be seen as orthogonal to this model and the authors need to clarify and justify how their data relates.

h) Subsection “Experiment 5: Lexical decision task” – why is the model retrained? If the model based on letters in general is used in this task shouldn't the same weights be used?

i) The summary sentence "In sum, we conclude that word response times are explained by word frequency and nonword response times are explained by the distance between the nonword and the nearest word calculated using the compositional neural code." accurately captures what the data show. It highlights how the authors' model makes interesting predictions in a variety of contexts. But it also contradicts the main assertions laid out in the Introduction as they note that many factors that are not purely visual explain a major portion of the variance.

j) Some of the findings on the fMRI task have been reported a number of times in the literature (e.g. the difference in VWFA response to words and pseudowords). The manuscript would be strengthened by relating it to these previous studies.

3) The authors find that LO is the region that is most sensitive to their visual similarity metric.

a) Given prior work showing the critical role of VWFA in reading, this result would seem to suggest that visual similarity is not at the core of reading per se and this issue should be discussed.

b) The paragraph beginning with "To further investigate the link between the compositional…" needs clarifying. Further, prior work has focused on the VWFA for the claim of bigram detectors and the authors needs to explain how the finding of a compositional code in LO relates to that work.

c) The authors also show that LO has a representation of semantic space. This suggests a contribution beyond visual properties. What does this mean for the role of these neurons? What are the implications of this overlap for theories of orthographic and semantic processing? This needs to be discussed.

4) Some results do not seem to support the ideas of the paper, but are framed as doing so. Specifically:

a) "To quantify this observation, we asked whether the model error for each bigram pair, calculated as the absolute difference between observed and predicted dissimilarity, covaried with the average bigram frequency of the two bigrams (for both frequent bigrams and words). […] We conclude that bigram search can be explained entirely using single neurons tuned to single letters."

The significant negative correlation does not seem to fit with the later statement that "model errors are not systematically different for frequent compared to infrequent bigram pairs". The authors should clarify this point in this paragraph, but also explain how this result fits with main message of the paper. There are a number of effects that are against the idea the main hypothesis "that word reading is enabled by a purely visual representation" and that the model "explained human performance in both visual search as well as word reading tasks." (Abstract). For instance, the effect of familiarity on asymmetric spatial summation (subsection “Experiment 3: Upright versus inverted bigrams”), and the frequency effect (Experiment 5).

b) If the claim is "there are no specialized detectors for letter combinations", it's not clear how Experiment 5 (where the same letters in different orders give different RTs) fits with this. This seems to strongly support a role for particular letter combinations.

5) In the analysis of mean VWFA activity, response times do not seem to be controlled. This is important because RTs might influence the magnitude of the β coefficients in a systematic way that does not directly correspond to the relevant processing. These should be included in the model.

6) In a number of places in the manuscript, the authors draw conclusions about how neurons are tuned, but without directly recording from neurons, it is not possible to draw this conclusion. For example, "Our main finding is that viewing a string activates a compositional letter code, consisting of neurons tuned to single letters whose response to longer strings is a linear sum of single letter responses".

7) It was mentioned that outliers in dissimilarity values across subjects were removed using built-in routines in MATLAB (isoutlier function, MATLAB R2018a). This is unusual and not typically seen in dissimilarity analyses. Are the findings the same without this procedure? How many outliers are removed? How is this threshold calculated/selected?

8) The manuscript mentions that cross-validation was performed but details on this are absent. In any case, pairwise dissimilarity calculations should be performed across runs (i.e., not correlating between items in the same run). This is particularly true because the trials are close together and influenced by the adjacent BOLD response.

9) It would be worth discussing how these findings relate to results (and associated theories) regarding whether individuals and specifically the VWFA process orthographic stimuli in a holistic versus part-based fashion (e.g., Carlos et al., 2019). More generally, behavioral responses to inverted words are relevant to this work, and worthy of more discussion (for how such findings are, or are not, consistent with this manuscript).

10) The authors report an exhaustive series of experiments and there is extensive supplementary material – while the authors should be commended for providing so much material, it does make the manuscript challenging to read at times, requiring the reader to jump around different parts of the text to fully understand the methods and results. The authors should include information such as the number of subjects in each experiment and key aspects of the stimuli (total number, how selected etc.), and protocol (e.g. timing of stimulus presentation, stimulus size etc.) in the main text. Further, there appears to be some inconsistency between the naming of sections. In the main text the authors refer the reader to, for example, "Section S7", but the supplementary material itself is labelled as "Section A7", and the tables and figures are numbered sequentially throughout the supplementary material such that the relevant figure in "Section A7" might be "Figure S16" – all very confusing. The authors should reconsider how they are structuring the supplementary material to make it more intuitively organized.

claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: The letter model yielded excellent fits to the observed bigram search data (r = 0.85, p<0.00005).
claims.source: This letter model yielded excellent fits to the observed data (r = 0.85, p<0.00005; Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on model fitting to the behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The letter model captured nearly all the systematic variance in the bigram search data.
claims.source: This consistency measure (rdata = 0.90) was close to the model fit, suggesting that the model captured nearly all the systematic variance in the data.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of model fit to data consistency.

claims.claim: The estimated spatial summation weights were unequal.
claims.source: As predicted in the schematic figure (Figure 3B), the estimated spatial summation weights were unequal (absolute difference between w1 and w2, mean ± sd: 0.07 ± 0.04).
claims.evidence: This is based on parameter estimation from the model fitting.

claims.claim: The absolute difference between spatial summation weights was significantly larger than for shuffled weights.
claims.source: The absolute difference between shuffled weights was significantly smaller than for the original weights (average absolute difference: 0.03 ± 0.02; p<0.005, sign-rank test across 10 neurons).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical comparison with shuffled control data.

claims.claim: Model errors are not systematically different for frequent compared to infrequent bigram pairs.
claims.source: This too revealed no systematic difference (mean ± sd of residual error: 0.10 ± 0.08 for the 20 most frequent bigrams and words; 0.11 ± 0.09 for 20 least frequent bigrams; p=0.80, rank-sum test).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model errors.

claims.claim: Bigram search can be explained entirely using single neurons tuned to single letters.
claims.source: We conclude that bigram search can be explained entirely using single neurons tuned to single letters.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model fitting results.

claims.claim: The response to transposed bigrams such as AB and BA will be different only if the summation weights are unequal.
claims.source: As detailed earlier, a critical prediction of this model is that the response to transposed bigrams such as AB and BA will be different only if the summation weights are unequal.
claims.evidence: This is a logical prediction from the model structure.

claims.claim: Repeated letter bigrams such as AA and BB will remain discriminable regardless of the nature of summation.
claims.source: By contrast, repeated letter bigrams such as AA and BB will remain discriminable regardless of the nature of summation, since their response will be proportional to the respective single letter responses.
claims.evidence: This is a logical prediction from the model structure.

claims.claim: Familiarity might modulate the summation to make it more asymmetric.
claims.source: Since reading expertise can modulate sensitivity to letter transpositions, we reasoned that familiarity might modulate the summation to make it more asymmetric.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on reasoning about reading expertise.

claims.claim: Transposed letter searches will be easier to discriminate in a familiar upright orientation compared to the unfamiliar inverted orientation.
claims.source: We therefore predicted that this would make transposed letter searches (with AB as target and BA as distractor, or vice-versa) easier to discriminate in a familiar upright orientation compared to the (unfamiliar) inverted orientation.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the familiarity hypothesis.

claims.claim: Searches involving repeated letter bigrams will remain equally easy in both upright and inverted orientations.
claims.source: By contrast, searches involving repeated letter bigrams (with AA as target and BB as distractor), which also have a change in two letters, will remain equally easy in both upright and inverted orientations.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the model structure.

claims.claim: Subjects discriminated repeated letter bigrams (AA-BB searches) equally well at both upright and inverted orientations.
claims.source: As predicted, subjects discriminated repeated letter bigrams (AA-BB searches) equally well at both upright and inverted orientations, but were substantially faster at discriminating transposed letter pairs (AB-BA searches) in the upright orientation (Figure 3D; for detailed analyses see Appendix 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on behavioral data from Experiment 3 shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Subjects were substantially faster at discriminating transposed letter pairs (AB-BA searches) in the upright orientation compared to inverted.
claims.source: As predicted, subjects discriminated repeated letter bigrams (AA-BB searches) equally well at both upright and inverted orientations, but were substantially faster at discriminating transposed letter pairs (AB-BA searches) in the upright orientation (Figure 3D; for detailed analyses see Appendix 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on behavioral data from Experiment 3 shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: There was a larger difference in the model summation weights for upright compared to inverted bigrams.
claims.source: Correspondingly, we observed a larger difference in the model summation weights for upright compared to inverted bigrams (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is based on model parameter estimation shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Familiarity leads to asymmetric spatial summation.
claims.source: We conclude that familiarity leads to asymmetric spatial summation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the upright vs inverted bigram results.

claims.claim: The single letter model yielded excellent fits to the six-letter string visual search data.
claims.source: The single letter model yielded excellent fits to the data (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is based on model fitting to the behavioral data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The letter model fits were superior to the Orthographic Levenshtein Distance (OLD) model.
claims.source: These fits were superior to a widely used measure of string similarity, the Orthographic Levenshtein Distance (OLD) model (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is based on model comparison shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The letter model fits were equivalent for both word-word pairs and nonword-nonword pairs.
claims.source: Importantly, the letter model fits were equivalent for both word-word pairs and nonword-nonword pairs (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is based on model fitting analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: Response times for nonwords will be inversely proportional to word frequency.
claims.source: We also predict that this comparison will be affected by the strength of the stored word representation, such that matches to frequent words are easier. In other words, we predict that response times for nonwords will be inversely proportional to word frequency.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the model.

claims.claim: When viewing the string 'PENCIL', the match to the stored word PENCIL takes no time and the response is dominated by word frequency.
claims.source: Finally, by the same account, when we view the string 'PENCIL', the match to the stored word PENCIL takes no time (the distance being negligible) and the response is therefore dominated by word frequency.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the model.

claims.claim: Subjects were highly accurate in responding to both words and nonwords in Experiment 5.
claims.source: Subjects were highly accurate in responding to both words and nonwords (mean ± sd: 96 ± 2% for words, 95 ± 3% for nonwords).
claims.evidence: This is based on behavioral data from Experiment 5.

claims.claim: Response times across words and nonwords were consistent between subjects in Experiment 5.
claims.source: Importantly, their response times across words and nonwords were consistent between subjects as evidenced by a significant split-half correlation (correlation between odd- and even-numbered subjects: r = 0.59 for words, r = 0.73 for nonwords, p<0.00005).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Response times for words showed a negative correlation with log word frequency (r = −0.5, p<0.00005).
claims.source: As predicted, response times for words showed a negative correlation with log word frequency (r = −0.5, p<0.00005 across 450 words).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Word frequency is the best predictor of word response times.
claims.source: It can be seen that the word frequency is the best predictor of word response times (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is based on cross-validated model comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The combined lexical model performance was slightly better than the performance of the word frequency model alone.
claims.source: To assess whether all lexical factors together predict word response times any better, we fit a combined model in which the word response times are modeled as a linear sum of the four factors. The combined model performance was slightly better than the performance of the word frequency model alone (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is based on cross-validated model comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Word response times are determined primarily by word frequency and to a lesser degree by letter frequency.
claims.source: We conclude that word response times are determined primarily by word frequency and to a lesser degree by letter frequency.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model comparison results.

claims.claim: The dependence of word response times on word frequency is non-compositional.
claims.source: We note that the dependence of word response times on word frequency is non-compositional, since it cannot be explained by letter frequency.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the model results.

claims.claim: The letter model yielded excellent fits to the nonword response time data (r = 0.70, p<0.00005).
claims.source: This model yielded excellent fits to the data (r = 0.70, p<0.00005; Figure 4E) that were comparable to the data consistency (rdata = 0.84).
claims.evidence: This is based on model fitting to the behavioral data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Subjects took longer to respond to nonwords obtained by transposing a letter of a word, compared to nonwords obtained through letter substitution.
claims.source: Specifically, subjects took longer to respond to nonwords obtained by transposing a letter of a word, compared to nonwords obtained through letter substitution – these trends were present in the model predictions as well (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is based on behavioral data and model predictions shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Subjects took longer when the middle letters were transposed compared to when the edge letters were transposed.
claims.source: Likewise, subjects took longer when the middle letters were transposed compared to when the edge letters were transposed – as did the model predictions (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is based on behavioral data and model predictions shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: These effects replicate the classic orthographic processing effects reported across many studies.
claims.source: These effects replicate the classic orthographic processing effects reported across many studies (Grainger et al., 2012; Norris, 2013; Ziegler et al., 2013; Grainger, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The OLD model yielded relatively poorer predictions of the nonword data (r = 0.36, p<0.00005).
claims.source: The OLD model yielded relatively poorer predictions of the data (r = 0.36, p<0.00005; Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is based on model fitting shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The letter model outperformed both the OLD model and the lexical model in predicting nonword response times.
claims.source: The letter model outperformed both the OLD model and the lexical model (model correlations: r = 0.56 ± 0.02, 0.33 ± 0.01 and 0.35 ± 0.01 for the neural, OLD and lexical models; fraction of bootstrap samples with neural <other models: p<0.005; Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This is based on cross-validated model comparison shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: The reduced SID model yielded fits that were better than the lexical model.
claims.source: Even this reduced model yielded fits were better than the lexical model (SID model correlation: r = 0.48 ± . 02).
claims.evidence: This is based on cross-validated model comparison.

claims.claim: The model trained on visual search data yielded a significant positive correlation with nonword response times (r = 0.39, p<0.00005).
claims.source: To assess whether the model trained on visual search data would also be able to predict nonword response times, we took the model trained on the visual search data in Experiment 4, and calculated the word-nonword distances using this model. This too yielded a significant positive correlation (r = 0.39, p<0.00005) that was better than the OLD and lexical models.
claims.evidence: This is based on cross-experiment model generalization.

claims.claim: A combined neural+lexical model explained more variance than either model alone.
claims.source: Finally, a combined model – in which the neural and lexical model predictions were linearly combined – proved to explain more variance than either model (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This is based on model comparison shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Word response times are explained primarily by word frequency.
claims.source: In sum, we conclude that word response times are explained primarily by word frequency and nonword response times are explained primarily by the distance between the nonword and the nearest word calculated using the compositional neural code.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lexical decision task results.

claims.claim: Nonword response times are explained primarily by the distance between the nonword and the nearest word calculated using the compositional neural code.
claims.source: In sum, we conclude that word response times are explained primarily by word frequency and nonword response times are explained primarily by the distance between the nonword and the nearest word calculated using the compositional neural code.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lexical decision task results.

claims.claim: The perceptual and semantic dissimilarities were uncorrelated (r = 0.03, p=0.55).
claims.source: Importantly, the perceptual and semantic dissimilarities were uncorrelated (r = 0.03, p=0.55), thereby allowing us to identify regions with distinct or overlapping perceptual/semantic representations.
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between perceptual and semantic dissimilarity measures.

claims.claim: Subjects were highly accurate in the fMRI lexical decision task (mean ±std of accuracy: 94 ± 4%).
claims.source: Subjects were highly accurate (mean ±std of accuracy: 94 ± 4%) and showed consistent response time variations (split-half correlation between odd and even subjects: rsh = 0.54 and 0.79 for words and nonwords, p<0.00005).
claims.evidence: This is based on behavioral data from Experiment 6.

claims.claim: Subjects showed consistent response time variations in the fMRI lexical decision task.
claims.source: Subjects were highly accurate (mean ±std of accuracy: 94 ± 4%) and showed consistent response time variations (split-half correlation between odd and even subjects: rsh = 0.54 and 0.79 for words and nonwords, p<0.00005).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: The lexical decision time for words was negatively correlated with word frequency (r = −0.42, p<0.05) in the fMRI experiment.
claims.source: As before, the lexical decision time for words was negatively correlated with word frequency (r = −0.42, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of the behavioral data from Experiment 6.

claims.claim: The lexical decision times for nonwords were strongly correlated with the word-nonword dissimilarity measured in visual search (r = −0.68, p<0.00005).
claims.source: Likewise, the lexical decision times for nonwords were strongly correlated with the word-nonword dissimilarity measured in visual search in Experiment 7 (r = −0.68, p<0.00005).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between Experiments 6 and 7.

claims.claim: VWFA and TG regions showed greater activation to nonwords compared to words.
claims.source: While V4 showed greater activation for words compared to nonwords, VWFA and TG regions showed greater activation to nonwords compared to words, presumably reflecting greater engagement to discriminate nonwords that are highly similar to words (Appendix 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on fMRI activation analysis.

claims.claim: Only the LO dissimilarities showed a significant correlation with perceptual dissimilarities (r = 0.16, p<0.00005).
claims.source: Among the ROIs tested, only the LO dissimilarities showed a significant correlation (correlation between 1024 pairwise dissimilarities involving 32C2 words, 32C2 nonwords, and 32 word-nonword pairs: r = 0.16, p<0.00005; Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between neural and perceptual dissimilarities shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: A searchlight analysis confirmed that the match to perceptual dissimilarities was strongest in a region centred around the bilateral LO region.
claims.source: A searchlight analysis confirmed that the match to perceptual dissimilarities was strongest in a region centred around the bilateral LO region (Appendix 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on searchlight analysis of the fMRI data.

claims.claim: LO is the likely neural substrate for the compositional letter code.
claims.source: Thus, neural dissimilarity in the LO region match best with the perceptual dissimilarities observed in visual search. We therefore conclude that LO is the likely neural substrate for the compositional letter code.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural dissimilarity analysis.

claims.claim: The match to semantic space was significant only in the LO and TG regions.
claims.source: The match to semantic space was significant only in the LO and TG regions (correlation between 496 pairwise dissimilarities between words: r = 0.18 ± 0.05 for LO, 0.22 ± 0.04 for TG; Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between neural and semantic dissimilarities shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: A searchlight analysis confirmed that semantic dissimilarities were best correlated with the TG region.
claims.source: A searchlight analysis confirmed that semantic dissimilarities were best correlated with the TG region with additional peaks in prefrontal and motor regions (Appendix 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on searchlight analysis of the fMRI data.

claims.claim: There is no significant difference between the neural representation in LO matching with perceptual or semantic space for word-word pairs.
claims.source: This revealed no significant difference between the two correlations (r = 0.16 ± . 04 for LO with visual search, r = 0.16 ± 0.05 for LO with semantic dissimilarites; p=0.49 across 1000 bootstrap samples).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of correlations.

claims.claim: Both LO and TG regions represent semantic space.
claims.source: We conclude that both LO and TG regions represent semantic space.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the semantic dissimilarity analysis.

claims.claim: Only the VWFA showed a consistently positive correlation with lexical decision times for both words and nonwords.
claims.source: Across the ROIs, only the VWFA showed a consistently positive correlation with lexical decision times for both words and nonwords (r = 0.52, p<0.005 for words; r = 0.47, p<0.05 for nonwords, Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between VWFA activity and lexical decision times shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: A searchlight analysis confirmed that there was a peak in the correlation with lexical decision times centred on the VWFA.
claims.source: A searchlight analysis confirmed that there was indeed a peak in the correlation with lexical decision times centred on the VWFA, with additional peaks in the parietal and frontal regions (Appendix 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on searchlight analysis of the fMRI data.

claims.claim: VWFA activations were larger for nonwords compared to words.
claims.source: Interestingly, VWFA activations were larger for nonwords compared to words (mean ± std of VWFA activations across subjects: 1.46 ± 0.22 for words, 2.03 ± 0.28 for nonwords; p<0.005, signed-rank test across 17 subject activations).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of VWFA activations.

claims.claim: VWFA activations were similar for transposed nonwords compared to substituted words.
claims.source: However, activations were similar for transposed nonwords compared to substituted words (mean ±std VWFA activations across subjects: 1.42 ± 0.33 for transposed nonwords, 1.38 ± 0.33 for substituted nonwords; p=0.62, signed-rank test).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of VWFA activations.

claims.claim: Lexical decisions are driven by the VWFA.
claims.source: We conclude that lexical decisions are driven by the VWFA.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the VWFA activation analysis.

claims.claim: Viewing a string of letters activates a compositional neural code in LO that is subsequently matched with stored word representations in the VWFA.
claims.source: This suggests that viewing a string of letters activates a compositional neural code in LO that is subsequently matched with stored word representations in the VWFA.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined fMRI results.

claims.claim: Existing models of reading assume explicit encoding of letter position and do not account for letter shape.
claims.source: Existing models of reading assume explicit encoding of letter position and do not account for letter shape (Gomez et al., 2008; Davis, 2010; Norris and Kinoshita, 2012; Norris, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The compositional letter code encodes letter shape explicitly and position implicitly through asymmetric spatial summation.
claims.source: By contrast, our model encodes letter shape explicitly and position implicitly through asymmetric spatial summation.
claims.evidence: This describes a key feature of the proposed model.

claims.claim: The implicit coding of letter position avoids the complication of counting transpositions.
claims.source: The implicit coding of letter position avoids the complication of counting transpositions (Yarkoni et al., 2008; Yap et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an advantage of the model supported by citations.

claims.claim: The compositional letter code is neurally plausible and grounded in well-known principles of object representations.
claims.source: Unlike existing models of reading, our compositional letter code is neurally plausible and grounded in well-known principles of object representations.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the model's theoretical foundation.

claims.claim: Images that elicit similar activity across neurons in high-level visual cortex will appear perceptually similar.
claims.source: The first principle is that images that elicit similar activity across neurons in high-level visual cortex will appear perceptually similar (Op de Beeck et al., 2001; Sripati and Olson, 2010a; Zhivago and Arun, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The neural response to multiple objects is typically the average of the individual object responses that can be biased toward a weighted sum.
claims.source: The second principle is that the neural response to multiple objects is typically the average of the individual object responses (Zoccolan et al., 2005; Sripati and Olson, 2010b) that can be biased toward a weighted sum (Ghose and Maunsell, 2008; Bao and Tsao, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The letter code assumes no explicit calculations of letter position in a word.
claims.source: Finally, we note that our letter code assumes no explicit calculations of letter position in a word, since the neurons in our model only need to be tuned for retinal position.
claims.evidence: This describes a key feature of the model.

claims.claim: Neurons may be tuned not only to retinal position but also to the relative size and position of letters.
claims.source: We speculate that these neurons may be tuned not only to retinal position but also to the relative size and position of letters, as observed in high-level visual cortex (Sripati and Olson, 2010a; Vighneshvel and Arun, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Lexical decisions for nonwords are driven by the dissimilarity between the viewed string and the nearest word.
claims.source: We have found that lexical decisions for nonwords are driven by the dissimilarity between the viewed string and the nearest word.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the lexical decision task.

claims.claim: This idea is consistent with the Interactive Activation model where viewing a string activates the nearest word representation.
claims.source: This idea is consistent with the well-known Interactive Activation model (McClelland and Rumelhart, 1981; Rumelhart and McClelland, 1982), where viewing a string activates the nearest word representation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous models.

claims.claim: The Interactive Activation model does not explain lexical decisions or scrambled word reading.
claims.source: However, the Interactive Activation model does not explain lexical decisions or scrambled word reading, and also does not integrate letter shape and position into a unified code.
claims.evidence: This is a limitation of previous models.

claims.claim: Nonword responses are influenced by the number of orthographic neighbors.
claims.source: Our findings are consistent with previous work showing that nonword responses are influenced by the number of orthographic neighbors (Yap et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Word frequency is a major factor influencing lexical decisions.
claims.source: Likewise, we found word frequency to be a major factor influencing lexical decisions, in keeping with previous work (Ratcliff et al., 2004; Dufau et al., 2012; Yap et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Personal familiarity with words might also influence lexical decisions.
claims.source: We note also that personal familiarity with words, as opposed to the word frequency estimated from text corpora, might also influence lexical decisions (Colombo et al., 2006; Kuperman and Van Dyke, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The compositional shape code provides a quick match to unscramble a word, failing which subjects may initiate more detailed symbolic manipulation.
claims.source: We propose that the compositional shape code provides a quick match to unscramble a word, failing which subjects may initiate more detailed symbolic manipulation.
claims.evidence: This is a proposal based on the study findings.

claims.claim: The success of the letter code challenges the widely held belief that efficient visual processing of letter strings requires higher-order detectors for letter combinations.
claims.source: The success of our letter code challenges the widely held belief that efficient visual processing of letter strings requires higher-order detectors for letter combinations (Grainger and Whitney, 2004; Dehaene et al., 2005; Dehaene et al., 2015; Grainger, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the implications of the findings, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The presence of specialized combination detectors should have caused larger model errors for valid words and frequent n-grams, but no such trend was observed.
claims.source: The presence of these specialized detectors should have caused larger model errors for valid words and frequent n-grams, but we observed no such trend (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of model errors shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: It is possible that there are combination detectors in subsequent stages where multiple letters have to activate single syllables.
claims.source: However, it is possible that there are combination detectors in subsequent stages where multiple letters have to activate single syllables.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about possible higher-level processing.

claims.claim: Reading should increase letter discrimination and increase the asymmetry of spatial summation.
claims.source: Our comparison of upright and inverted bigrams suggests that reading should increase letter discrimination and increase the asymmetry of spatial summation (Figure 3D,E).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the upright vs inverted bigram results.

claims.claim: This is consistent with the finding that reading makes words more predictable from letters.
claims.source: This is consistent with our recent finding that reading makes words more predictable from letters (Agrawal et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: This is consistent with differences in letter position effects for symbols and letters.
claims.source: It is also consistent with differences in letter position effects for symbols and letters (Chanceaux and Grainger, 2012; Scaltritti et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Both processes may be driven by visual exposure: repeated viewing of letters makes them more discriminable, while viewing letter combinations induces asymmetric spatial weighting or increased separability.
claims.source: We propose that both processes may be driven by visual exposure: repeated viewing of letters makes them more discriminable (Mruczek and Sheinberg, 2005), while viewing letter combinations induces asymmetric spatial weighting or increased separability.
claims.evidence: This is a proposal supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Perceptual dissimilarities between strings matched best with neural representations in the LO region.
claims.source: First, we found that perceptual dissimilarities between strings, regardless of word/nonword status, matched best with neural representations in the LO region (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is based on fMRI analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: This is consistent with similar findings using letters and natural objects.
claims.source: This is consistent with similar findings using letters (Agrawal et al., 2019) and natural objects (Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Semantic dissimilarities between words matched both with temporal gyrus regions as well as with LO.
claims.source: Second, we have found that semantic dissimilarities between words matched both with temporal gyrus regions as well as with LO (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is based on fMRI analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The finding that temporal gyrus regions match semantic dissimilarities is consistent with these regions participating in the reading network.
claims.source: The former finding is consistent with temporal gyrus regions participating in the reading network (Friederici and Gierhan, 2013), while the latter is concordant with other semantic properties such as animacy encoded in LO (Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2016; Proklova et al., 2016; Thorat et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The finding that LO matches semantic dissimilarities is concordant with other semantic properties such as animacy encoded in LO.
claims.source: The former finding is consistent with temporal gyrus regions participating in the reading network (Friederici and Gierhan, 2013), while the latter is concordant with other semantic properties such as animacy encoded in LO (Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2016; Proklova et al., 2016; Thorat et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Whether semantic properties are encoded directly by LO or are a consequence of feedback from language/semantic areas can be distinguished using methods with higher temporal resolution.
claims.source: Whether these semantic properties are encoded directly by LO or are a consequence of feedback from language/semantic areas can be distinguished using methods with higher temporal resolution such as MEG or intracranial recordings.
claims.evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claims.claim: There is a striking correlation between lexical decision times for words as well as nonwords in the VWFA.
claims.source: We found a striking correlation between lexical decision times for words as well as nonwords in the VWFA (Figure 5E), suggesting that it is involved in comparing the viewed string with stored words.
claims.evidence: This is based on fMRI analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: VWFA is involved in comparing the viewed string with stored words.
claims.source: We found a striking correlation between lexical decision times for words as well as nonwords in the VWFA (Figure 5E), suggesting that it is involved in comparing the viewed string with stored words.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between VWFA activity and lexical decision times.

claims.claim: The finding that VWFA activity is positively correlated with word response times is consistent with previous studies showing that VWFA activity shows weak activity for frequent words.
claims.source: The finding that VWFA activity is positively correlated with word response times (which reflect word frequency as shown in Figure 4C) is consistent with previous studies showing that VWFA activity shows weak activity for frequent words (Kronbichler et al., 2004; Vinckier et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The finding that VWFA activity is correlated with nonword response times is consistent with observations that VWFA is modulated by orthographic similarity to words.
claims.source: The finding that VWFA activity is correlated with nonword response times (which reflect perceptual distance to the corresponding word, as shown in Figure 5E), is consistent with observations that VWFA is modulated by orthographic similarity to words (Vinckier et al., 2007; Baeck et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The finding that VWFA activations were stronger for nonwords compared to words has also been observed recently.
claims.source: Finally, our finding that VWFA activations were stronger for nonwords compared to words (Figure 5E), has also been observed recently (Bouhali et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claims.claim: The higher activity for nonwords is likely due to many of them being perceptually similar to words, making the lexical decision difficult.
claims.source: While this might seem paradoxical considering its status as a word form area, the higher activity for nonwords is likely due to many of them being perceptually similar to words, making the lexical decision difficult.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the VWFA activation pattern.

claims.claim: VWFA is activated strongly for hard lexical decisions, which is concordant with its higher activation for inverted compared to upright words while making lexical decisions.
claims.source: That VWFA is activated strongly for hard lexical decisions is also concordant with its higher activation for inverted compared to upright words while making lexical decisions (Carlos et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Some studies have reported equal activity in VWFA for words and nonwords.
claims.source: Some studies have reported equal activity in VWFA for words and nonwords (Baker et al., 2007), and others have reported higher activity for word-like stimuli (Vinckier et al., 2007; Glezer et al., 2009) – but these observations have been made while subjects performed tasks orthogonal to reading.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: There have been surprisingly few studies of VWFA activations during word processing tasks.
claims.source: There have been surprisingly few studies of VWFA activations during word processing tasks (Baeck et al., 2015; Sussman et al., 2018; Bouhali et al., 2019; Carlos et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Orthographic (perceptual) similarity between strings was encoded not by VWFA but by LO.
claims.source: By comparing brain activations directly with behavioral responses during a lexical decision task, we found an interesting functional dissociation whereby orthographic (perceptual) similarity between strings was encoded not by VWFA but by LO (Figure 5C) and lexical decisions were encoded by VWFA and not LO (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is based on fMRI analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5F.

claims.claim: Lexical decisions were encoded by VWFA and not LO.
claims.source: By comparing brain activations directly with behavioral responses during a lexical decision task, we found an interesting functional dissociation whereby orthographic (perceptual) similarity between strings was encoded not by VWFA but by LO (Figure 5C) and lexical decisions were encoded by VWFA and not LO (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is based on fMRI analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5F.

claims.claim: Most orthographic processing phenomena are driven by compositional neural representations in LO, rather than by the VWFA.
claims.source: This finding implies that most orthographic processing phenomena are driven by compositional neural representations in LO, rather than by the VWFA.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the functional dissociation between LO and VWFA.

claims.claim: These findings are consistent with recent intracranial EEG recordings that report a progression from early to late, or letter-level to word-level representations along the ventral occipitotemporal cortex regions.
claims.source: These findings are consistent with recent intracranial EEG recordings that report a progression from early to late, or letter-level to word-level representations along the ventral occipitotemporal cortex regions (Thesen et al., 2012; Hirshorn et al., 2016; Lochy et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The letter code's integrated representation of both letter shape and position explains both letter transposition and substitution effects and their relative importance.
claims.source: Its integrated representation of both letter shape and position explains both letter transposition and substitution effects and their relative importance (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is based on model predictions shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The letter code's asymmetric spatial weighting favoring the first letter explains the first-letter advantage observed previously.
claims.source: Its asymmetric spatial weighting favoring the first letter (Appendix 3), explains the first-letter advantage observed previously (Scaltritti et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The letter code explains why increasing letter spacing can benefit reading in poor readers.
claims.source: It also explains why increasing letter spacing can benefit reading in poor readers, presumably because it increases asymmetry in spatial summation (Zorzi et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Transposing the edge letters results in a bigger change than transposing the middle letters according to the letter model.
claims.source: It can be seen transposing the edge letters (OFRGET) results in a bigger change than transposing the middle letters (FOGRET), thus explaining many transposed letter effects (Norris, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is based on model predictions shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Substituting a dissimilar letter leads to a large change compared to substituting a similar letter according to the letter model.
claims.source: Likewise, it can be seen that substituting a dissimilar letter (FORXET) leads to a large change compared to substituting a similar letter (FORCET).
claims.evidence: This is based on model predictions shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Replacing G with C in FORGET leads to a smaller change than replacing with X, thus explaining how priming is stronger when similar letters are substituted.
claims.source: Replacing G with C in FORGET leads to a smaller change than replacing with X, thus explaining how priming is stronger when similar letters are substituted (Marcet and Perea, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on model predictions and supported by citation.

claims.claim: The letter subset FRGT is closer to FORGET than the same letters reversed (TGRF), thereby explaining subset priming.
claims.source: Finally, the letter subset FRGT is closer to FORGET than the same letters reversed (TGRF), thereby explaining subset priming (Grainger and Whitney, 2004; Dehaene et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is based on model predictions and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The compositional neural code can serve as a powerful baseline for the purely visual shape-based representation triggered by viewing words.
claims.source: We propose that this compositional neural code can serve as a powerful baseline for the purely visual shape-based representation triggered by viewing words, thereby enabling the study of higher order linguistic influences on reading processes.
claims.evidence: This is a proposal about the utility of the model.

claims.claim: Reading sentences is much more complex than reading single words, with potentially many words sampled with each eye movement.
claims.source: Our results constitute an important first step in understanding how we read single words, but reading sentences is much more complex, with potentially many words sampled with each eye movement (Rayner, 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Our ability to sample multiple letters or words at a single glance is limited by visual acuity and crowding.
claims.source: Our ability to sample multiple letters or words at a single glance is limited by two factors. The first is our visual acuity, which reduces with eccentricity. The second is crowding, by which letters become unrecognizable when flanked by other letters – this effect increases with eccentricity (Pelli and Tillman, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The finding that visual search dissimilarity explains word recognition implies that shape representations are qualitatively similar in the fovea and periphery.
claims.source: Our finding that visual search dissimilarity explains word recognition then implies that shape representations are qualitatively similar in the fovea and periphery.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the study findings.

claims.source: Furthermore, the structure of the letter model suggests a possible mechanistic explanation for crowding.

claims.source: Neural responses might show greater sensitivity to spatial location at the fovea compared to the periphery, leading to more discriminable representations of multiple letters.

results.result: A compositional neural code based on linear summation of letter responses can explain human performance on visual search and jumbled word reading tasks. The model predicts dissimilarities between letter strings that match behavioral data from both visual search (C5) and word reading tasks (C6), supporting the hypothesis that viewing jumbled words activates a visual representation compared to known words (C3).
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C6 and C9 form a coherent result supported by behavioral data from multiple experiments. The compositional model (C4) successfully predicts performance across visual search (C5, r=0.85-0.87) and lexical decision tasks (C6, r=0.70), with high correlations approaching data consistency limits. The model's success across different tasks provides converging evidence for the compositional neural code hypothesis.

results.result: The lateral occipital (LO) region is the neural substrate for the compositional letter code. Neural dissimilarities in LO matched perceptual dissimilarities from visual search (r=0.16, p<0.00005), confirmed by searchlight analysis showing strongest match centered on bilateral LO.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C80-C82, and C115 collectively establish LO as the neural substrate for the letter code. The correlation between LO neural dissimilarities and perceptual dissimilarities (C80) is statistically significant and confirmed by independent searchlight analysis (C81). However, the correlation magnitude (r=0.16) is modest, suggesting other factors may contribute. The result is supported but the effect size warrants noting.

results.result: The visual word form area (VWFA) is involved in lexical decisions by comparing viewed strings with stored word representations. VWFA showed consistent positive correlation with lexical decision times for both words (r=0.52, p<0.005) and nonwords (r=0.47, p<0.05), confirmed by searchlight analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C87-C88, C91, C121-C122 establish VWFA's role in lexical decisions. The correlations between VWFA activity and decision times are statistically significant for both words and nonwords (C87), with searchlight confirmation (C88). The interpretation that VWFA compares strings to stored words (C122) is a reasonable inference from the correlation pattern, though alternative explanations exist.

results.result: Multidimensional scaling (MDS) of single letter visual search data reconstructs artificial neurons tuned for letter shape. Subjects showed high consistency (r=0.87, p<0.00005), and letter dissimilarities correlated with previous subjective ratings. MDS dimensions represent putative neural responses, with increasing dimensions improving match to observed dissimilarities.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C32 describe the MDS methodology and validation. High inter-subject consistency (C27) and correlation with independent ratings (C28) validate the approach. The MDS reconstruction (C30-C31) is mathematically sound, though the specific neural interpretation is one of multiple possible solutions (acknowledged in text). The increasing fit with dimensions (C32) follows expected MDS behavior.

results.result: Bigram visual search can be explained entirely using single letter responses with asymmetric spatial summation. The letter model achieved excellent fits (r=0.85, p<0.00005), capturing nearly all systematic variance (data consistency r=0.90). Spatial summation weights were significantly unequal (p<0.005), and letter transpositions were more similar than substitutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C40 demonstrate that bigram search is explained by single letter tuning. The model fit (C35, r=0.85) approaches data consistency (C36, r=0.90), indicating near-optimal performance. Unequal summation weights (C37-C38) are statistically validated against shuffled controls. The finding that transpositions are more similar than substitutions (C33) replicates classic reading effects. The conclusion (C40) is well-supported.

results.result: The letter model shows no systematic differences in errors for frequent versus infrequent bigrams or for words versus nonwords, challenging the need for specialized combination detectors. Model errors were equivalent across frequency conditions (p=0.80) and word status.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C52, and C109 provide evidence against specialized bigram/word detectors. The lack of systematic error differences for frequent bigrams (C39) and words (C52) is statistically demonstrated. This challenges prevailing theories requiring higher-order detectors (C109). However, the analysis is limited to visual search and may not capture all aspects of reading. The result is supported within its scope.

results.result: Familiarity with letter orientation leads to asymmetric spatial summation. Subjects discriminated transposed letter pairs (AB-BA) faster in upright versus inverted orientation, while repeated letter pairs (AA-BB) showed no orientation effect. Model summation weights showed larger asymmetry for upright bigrams.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C49 test and confirm the familiarity hypothesis. The predicted interaction between letter type and orientation (C44-C45) was observed (C46-C47), with corresponding model parameter differences (C48). The experimental design appropriately controls for low-level factors by comparing repeated versus transposed pairs. The conclusion about familiarity (C49) is supported, though the mechanism (visual vs. linguistic familiarity) remains unclear.

results.result: The letter model generalizes to six-letter strings, yielding excellent fits that are superior to the Orthographic Levenshtein Distance (OLD) model and equivalent for word-word and nonword-nonword pairs.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 demonstrate model generalization. The fits are described as excellent (C50) and superior to OLD (C51), with equivalent performance across word types (C52). However, specific correlation values are not provided in these claims, making quantitative assessment difficult. The result is supported but would benefit from explicit statistics.

results.result: Word response times in lexical decision are determined primarily by word frequency (r=-0.5, p<0.00005), with lesser contribution from letter frequency. Cross-validated model comparison showed word frequency as the best single predictor, with combined lexical model performing slightly better.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C61 and C72 establish word frequency as the primary factor for word responses. High accuracy (C56) and inter-subject consistency (C57) validate the data. The correlation with word frequency (C58) is substantial and confirmed by cross-validated model comparison (C59-C60). The conclusion (C61, C72) is well-supported, though the non-compositional nature (C62) is a logical inference rather than direct evidence.

results.result: Nonword response times are explained primarily by the distance between the nonword and nearest word calculated using the compositional neural code (r=0.70, p<0.00005). The model captured classic orthographic effects (transposition vs. substitution, middle vs. edge) and outperformed OLD and lexical models in cross-validated comparison.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66, C68, and C73 demonstrate the letter model's success for nonwords. The model fit (C63, r=0.70) is substantial and approaches data consistency (r=0.84). Classic orthographic effects are replicated (C64-C66), and cross-validated comparison shows superiority over alternatives (C68). The conclusion (C73) is well-supported. However, the model was fit to the lexical decision data, which may inflate performance estimates.

results.result: The letter model trained on visual search data generalizes to predict nonword response times (r=0.39, p<0.00005), better than OLD and lexical models. A combined neural+lexical model explained more variance than either alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 demonstrate cross-task generalization. The correlation (C70, r=0.39) is significant and represents true prediction since the model was trained on independent visual search data. The combined model (C71) shows complementary contributions of visual and lexical factors. This is strong evidence for the model's validity, though the correlation is modest.

results.result: In the fMRI lexical decision task, subjects were highly accurate (94±4%) with consistent response times. Word decision times correlated negatively with word frequency (r=-0.42, p<0.05), and nonword decision times correlated strongly with word-nonword dissimilarity from visual search (r=-0.68, p<0.00005). Perceptual and semantic dissimilarities were uncorrelated (r=0.03, p=0.55).
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C78 establish the fMRI behavioral data quality and replicate key findings. High accuracy and consistency (C75-C76) validate the data. The correlations with word frequency (C77) and perceptual dissimilarity (C78) replicate out-of-scanner findings. The lack of correlation between perceptual and semantic spaces (C74) is important for dissociating neural representations. All results are statistically supported.

results.result: Semantic dissimilarities between words matched significantly with neural representations in both LO (r=0.18±0.05) and temporal gyrus (TG, r=0.22±0.04) regions, confirmed by searchlight analysis showing strongest correlation with TG.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84, C86, and C117 establish semantic representation in LO and TG. The correlations are statistically significant (C83) and confirmed by searchlight analysis (C84). However, the correlation magnitudes are modest (r~0.18-0.22), and the interpretation that both regions 'represent' semantic space (C86) may overstate the strength of evidence. The result is supported but the effect sizes are small.

results.result: For word-word pairs, there is no significant difference between LO neural representation matching with perceptual versus semantic space (both r=0.16, p=0.49).
results.evaluation: Claim C85 shows equivalent correlations between LO and perceptual/semantic spaces for words. The statistical comparison (p=0.49) appropriately tests the difference. This suggests LO encodes both types of information for words, though the modest correlation magnitudes (r=0.16) indicate substantial unexplained variance. The result is supported but limited in scope.

results.result: VWFA activations were larger for nonwords compared to words (1.46±0.22 vs. 2.03±0.28, p<0.005), but similar for transposed versus substituted nonwords (1.42±0.33 vs. 1.38±0.33, p=0.62).
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 report VWFA activation patterns. The word/nonword difference (C89) is statistically significant and replicated in recent literature (C125). The lack of difference between transposition types (C90) is also statistically supported. These patterns are interpreted as reflecting task difficulty (C126), which is plausible but not directly tested. The results are supported.

results.result: Viewing letter strings activates a compositional neural code in LO that is subsequently matched with stored word representations in VWFA. This functional dissociation shows orthographic similarity encoded in LO, while lexical decisions are encoded in VWFA, implying most orthographic processing phenomena are driven by LO rather than VWFA.
results.evaluation: Claims C92, C130-C132 synthesize the fMRI findings into a processing model. The functional dissociation (C130-C131) is supported by the differential correlations of LO with perceptual space and VWFA with decision times. The inference that orthographic processing is driven by LO (C132) follows logically. However, this is a correlational result that doesn't establish causal relationships or temporal sequence. The result is supported within these limitations.

results.result: The compositional letter code differs from existing reading models by encoding letter shape explicitly and position implicitly through asymmetric spatial summation, avoiding complications of counting transpositions. The model is neurally plausible and grounded in principles of object representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 contrast the proposed model with existing theories. The characterization of existing models (C93) is supported by citations. The model's features (C94-C95) are accurately described and represent genuine differences. The claim of neural plausibility (C96) is supported by the model's basis in established neural principles (C24-C26, C97-C98). This is a valid theoretical contribution.

results.result: The success of the letter code challenges the belief that efficient visual processing of letter strings requires higher-order detectors for letter combinations. No systematic trend of larger model errors for valid words and frequent n-grams was observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109 challenge prevailing theories. The lack of systematic errors for frequent combinations (C109, also C39, C52) provides evidence against specialized detectors. However, this is negative evidence (absence of effect), which is weaker than positive evidence. The challenge to existing theories (C108) is justified but should be considered provisional pending additional tests. The result is supported but requires further validation.

results.result: Reading expertise should increase letter discrimination and asymmetry of spatial summation, consistent with findings that reading makes words more predictable from letters and with differences in letter position effects for symbols versus letters. Both processes may be driven by visual exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C114 propose mechanisms for reading expertise effects. The inference from upright/inverted bigrams (C111) is reasonable but speculative. The consistency with previous findings (C112-C113) provides indirect support, but these are correlational observations. The proposed mechanism (C114) is speculative and not directly tested. This represents a plausible hypothesis requiring further experimental validation.

results.result: The letter code explains multiple orthographic processing phenomena: transposition and substitution effects (C134), first-letter advantage (C135), benefits of letter spacing (C136), edge versus middle letter effects (C137), similar letter substitution effects (C138-C139), and subset priming (C140).
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C140 demonstrate the model's explanatory scope. The model predictions for various phenomena are shown in Figure 6A and match literature findings (supported by citations C135-C136, C139-C140). However, these are post-hoc explanations rather than a priori predictions, which limits their evidential value. The model's ability to account for diverse phenomena is impressive but should be validated through prospective predictions.

results.result: Lexical decisions for nonwords are driven by dissimilarity to the nearest word, consistent with the Interactive Activation model but extending it to explain lexical decisions and integrate letter shape and position. Findings are consistent with previous work on orthographic neighbors and word frequency effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C105 relate findings to existing theories. The consistency with Interactive Activation (C102) and previous findings (C104-C105) is supported by citations and data (C58, C63). The claim that the current model extends beyond Interactive Activation (C103) is justified by the integration of shape and position. This represents a valid theoretical contribution building on established frameworks.

results.result: The finding that visual search dissimilarity explains word recognition implies shape representations are qualitatively similar in fovea and periphery. The letter model structure suggests possible mechanistic explanations for crowding through differential spatial sensitivity or predictability of multi-letter responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C148 extend the model to peripheral vision and crowding. The inference about foveal/peripheral similarity (C144) is logical but not directly tested. The proposed crowding mechanisms (C145-C148) are speculative and not empirically validated. These represent interesting hypotheses but require experimental testing. The result is uncertain pending further evidence.

results.result: Jumbled word reading is effortless (demonstrated by Cambridge effect), but neural correlates are poorly understood. Visual search examples show FOGRET is harder to find than OFRGET among FORGET, indicating FOGRET is more visually similar to FORGET, potentially explaining why transposing middle letters makes words easier to read than transposing edge letters.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C18-C22 establish the motivation and initial observations. The Cambridge effect (C1) is well-documented. The visual search example (C18-C20) provides intuitive demonstration, and the inference about reading difficulty (C21-C22) is logical. However, these are preliminary observations rather than systematic evidence. The result is supported as motivation but requires the subsequent experiments for validation.

results.result: Orthographic processing can potentially be explained by purely visual processing without invoking linguistic factors.
results.evaluation: Claim C23 is a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated result. While the subsequent experiments provide support for visual factors, they don't exclude linguistic contributions (indeed, C71 shows combined models perform best). The claim is too strong given that subjects may have been reading during visual search (acknowledged in text). This remains uncertain as a general principle.

results.result: Word reading is influenced by multiple factors: visual (similar shapes, preserved first/last letters, fewer transpositions, preserved word shape) and linguistic (word frequency, bigram/trigram frequency, preserved consonant clusters/morphemes).
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C17 summarize prior literature on reading factors. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to previous work. This represents accurate characterization of the field rather than new findings. The result is supported as background knowledge.

results.result: The model is based on established neural principles: perceptually similar images elicit similar neural activity, neural responses to multiple objects average individual responses (biased toward weighted sum), and neurons in high-level visual cortex are tuned for letter shape and retinal position.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 and C97-C98 establish the neural basis of the model. All principles are supported by appropriate citations to neurophysiology literature. These represent established findings rather than new discoveries. The result is supported as theoretical foundation.

results.result: Perceptual dissimilarities matched best with LO (consistent with previous findings), while semantic dissimilarities matched with both TG (consistent with reading network participation) and LO (consistent with animacy encoding).
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C119 relate findings to previous literature. The consistency with prior work (C116, C118-C119) is supported by appropriate citations. This represents replication and extension of established findings. The result is supported.

results.result: VWFA shows striking correlation with lexical decision times for words and nonwords, suggesting involvement in comparing viewed strings with stored words. This is consistent with previous findings of weak activity for frequent words, modulation by orthographic similarity, and stronger activation for nonwords and inverted words during lexical decisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C127 establish VWFA function and relate to literature. The correlations (C121, also C87) are statistically significant. The interpretation (C122) is reasonable though inferential. The consistency with previous findings (C123-C125, C127) is well-documented. The explanation for higher nonword activity (C126) is plausible. The result is supported.

results.result: Previous studies show mixed findings on VWFA activity for words versus nonwords, but few studies examined VWFA during word processing tasks. Current findings are consistent with intracranial EEG showing progression from letter-level to word-level representations along ventral occipitotemporal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129 and C133 contextualize findings in literature. The characterization of previous mixed findings (C128-C129) is accurate and supported by citations. The consistency with intracranial recordings (C133) provides converging evidence. This represents appropriate literature integration.

results.result: The compositional neural code can serve as a powerful baseline for purely visual shape-based representation triggered by viewing words, enabling study of higher-order linguistic influences on reading.
results.evaluation: Claim C141 proposes utility of the model for future research. This is a reasonable proposal given the model's demonstrated ability to explain visual factors. The claim is modest (serving as a baseline) and supported by the empirical findings. However, this is a prospective claim about future utility rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: Reading sentences is more complex than single words, with multiple words sampled per eye movement. Ability to sample multiple letters/words is limited by visual acuity and crowding, both increasing with eccentricity.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C143 acknowledge limitations and context. These are well-established facts supported by appropriate citations. This represents accurate characterization of the broader reading context rather than new findings.
